issues.failure_explanation: The equivalence G(∞)=0 ⇔ C+D=0 rests on the leading-order ratio (C+D)/(C−D/2), which needs C−D/2≠0, i.e. (C,D)≠(0,0). This hypothesis is never stated. At C=D=0 the condition C+D=0 holds, but Stage 2 reduces to G(z)=(1+z[1/6+(2/3)R(z)])/(1−z/6), and since R(∞)=1 this gives G(∞)=−5≠0. So the 'if' direction is false.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the lemma for (C,D)≠(0,0), or add the case C=D=0 with the computation G(∞)=−5.
issues.overall_effect: Only the degenerate point (C,D)=(0,0) is affected. The final parameter interval C≥0.0188 never uses it, so the later results are unchanged.
issues.title: Lemma 3.1 'if and only if' fails at the degenerate point C=D=0
issues.why_classification: A one-line hypothesis or case fix removes the defect, and no substantive claim is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: So that the real part of $z$ is

issues.failure_explanation: The formula Re z=(1/3+13C)/(6C) holds only when the discriminant is negative (complex-conjugate roots). For C<0 the discriminant (1/3+13C)^2−24C is positive, so the roots are real. Their product is 2/(3C)<0, so one root is negative and G has a pole in the closed left half-plane. For example, C=−1 gives roots ≈4.59 and ≈−0.145. Hence 'Re z>0 for C<−1/39' is false, and analyticity of G in Re z≤0 holds only for C≥0.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use Vieta's formulas (product 2/(3C), sum (1/3+13C)/(3C)) to show that all poles lie in Re z>0 iff C≥0, and drop the C<−1/39 branch.
issues.overall_effect: Lemma 3.2 as stated is false for C<−1/39. The final A-stability interval lies in C>0, so the paper's conclusions do not depend on the wrong part.
issues.title: Lemma 3.2 wrongly allows C<-1/39: for C<0 one pole of G lies in the left half-plane
issues.why_classification: A short local argument corrects the lemma, and the result actually used (C>0) and the final interval are unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Analytically proving $\lvert G(iy)\lvert\leq 1$ for all $y\in\mathbb{R}$ is complex. Instead, we employ a systematic numerical scanning algorithm to determine the A-stability conditions of the scheme.
The parameter space $C \in [0.00, 0.10]$ is discretized into 5,000 sampling points
the frequency domain along the imaginary axis $y\in [10^{-8}, 10^{4}]$ is densely sampled using 25,000 logarithmically spaced points
a sufficient condition for A-stability is established through systematic theoretical and numerical investigation

issues.failure_explanation: Condition 2, sup_y |G(iy)|≤1, is checked only at finitely many (C,y) grid points; no analytic bound is given. The paper nonetheless states, as a result, that the scheme 'achieves A-stability' for C∈[0.018824,0.045589], and the abstract calls this a 'sufficient condition … established'. The scan cannot certify the inequality for all y and all C in the interval. Since the scheme has order 4 and real coefficients, |G(iy)|^2−1=O(y^6), so for small y the deviation from 1 is far below double-precision resolution and the sign cannot be determined numerically. The endpoints are quoted to six digits, but the C-grid spacing is about 2×10^-5, so the exact endpoints are not established.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either prove |G(iy)|^2≤1 for all y (a polynomial inequality in y^2 and C, including the small-y expansion) over the stated interval, or restate the conclusion as numerically observed on the scanned grid with the endpoints given only to the scan resolution.
issues.overall_effect: The central stability guarantee (A-stability on a specific C-interval) is only numerically observed, not proven. The advertised 'sufficient condition' and the final scheme with C∈[0.018824,0.045589] are unverified as A-stable.
issues.title: A-stability asserted for an interval of C on the basis of a finite floating-point scan, not a proof
issues.why_classification: A contained analytic argument or an honest weakening restores a comparable result, and no new global architecture is needed.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where $C \in [0.018824, 0.045589]$, with $C=0.018924$ being the optimal value.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper defines no objective for 'optimal' (for example minimising the error constant, or a bound on |G| over some region) and reports no computation comparing values of C. It gives no evidence for 'superior numerical damping'. The value lies within 10^-4 of the lower endpoint of the scanned stability interval, where the margin of A-stability is smallest, and nothing shows that damping there is better than elsewhere in the interval. The numerical tests use this C without any comparison against other C.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Define an explicit optimality criterion and show the computation, or call C=0.018924 an empirically chosen value without optimality claims.
issues.overall_effect: The recommended parameter in the final scheme is unjustified. The scheme remains consistent and fourth-order for any admissible C.
issues.title: 'Optimal' parameter C=0.018924 is asserted without any optimality criterion or analysis
issues.why_classification: Rewording or a short supporting computation suffices, and the scheme, its order and its stability interval are unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: our scheme reduces the numerical error by about an order of magnitude under identical time steps and offers superior stability that enables even larger step sizes.
focusing on stable time step size and convergence error, to verify the superiority of the former

issues.failure_explanation: Section 5 only tabulates errors of Implicit TSFO and 'Implicit RK4' at identical step sizes, all of which are stable for both methods. No stability limit, stability region or maximal stable step is computed for either method. The explicit RK4 appears only to generate the reference solution, so no comparison with explicit RK4 exists. The 'Implicit RK4' scheme is never specified. If it is an A-stable fourth-order implicit RK method, its stability region equals the whole left half-plane, the same as the A-stable TSFO, so 'superior stability regions' is unsupported. The 'order of magnitude smaller error' claim also fails in several tables (Robertson τ/8, Van der Pol τ=10^-2, Ozone t=321.8122 at τ=0.5), where RK4 is more accurate.

failure_location.quote: Comparisons with classical explicit and implicit fourth-order Runge-Kutta methods demonstrate that the proposed scheme possesses superior stability regions and smaller numerical errors.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Specify the implicit RK4 method and add a stability-region or maximal-step comparison, including explicit RK4. Otherwise remove or weaken the claims of 'superior stability regions' and 'order of magnitude' error reduction.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised advantages over classical explicit and implicit RK4 (stability and uniform accuracy gains) are not demonstrated. Only asymptotic fourth-order convergence and comparable or somewhat smaller errors are shown.
issues.title: Claims of superior stability regions and of comparison with explicit RK4 are not supported by the experiments
issues.why_classification: The claim can be withdrawn or backed by contained additional analysis or experiments, leaving a comparable result, but this requires more than rewording.
